node.label: Luisa Passerini
node.date_label: Work Ideology and Consensus (1979) · Torino operaia e fascismo (1984; English 1987) · Autoritratto di gruppo (1988; English 1996) · Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999) · Memoria e utopia (2003; English 2007)
node.description: Passerini argued that workers’ memories of fascism reveal cultural identities and everyday negotiations with power, rather than offering a direct measure of consent or resistance. Torino operaia e fascismo (1984), translated as Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), combines life histories with other sources to interpret those meanings. Richard Cándida Smith praised its method but questioned how cultural resistance became political action and how clearly it separated attitudes from the fascist period from later recollection (1988). Paul Thompson later said that by the second edition of The Voice of the Past (1988) oral historians had been strongly influenced by her ideas on subjectivity, silence and memory. Joan Wallach Scott introduced the English Autobiography of a Generation (1996), which interweaves the author’s recollections with other participants’ memories of 1968. With Selma Leydesdorff and Thompson, Passerini also made gendered memory a collaborative question, warning against universal differences between men and women (1996). Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999) extended her inquiry to emotions and European belonging: Timothy Bewes criticized its lack of a unified object, consistent method and explicit thesis; her reply defended historical discontinuity and the interpretation of neglected traces (2000). Her later publications include Memoria e utopia (2003; English 2007).
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Work Ideology and Consensus under Italian Fascism” (1979); Torino operaia e fascismo (1984), translated as Fascism in Popular Memory (1987); Autoritratto di gruppo (1988), translated by Lisa Erdberg as Autobiography of a Generation: Italy, 1968 (1996), foreword by Joan Wallach Scott; Memory and Totalitarianism (ed., 1992); Gender and Memory (coed. with Selma Leydesdorff and Paul Thompson, 1996; new Leydesdorff introduction, 2005); Europe in Love, Love in Europe (1999); Memoria e utopia (2003), English Memory and Utopia (2007).
node.scope_note: Read Fascism in Popular Memory only in the publisher’s Introduction excerpt, pp. 1–10; Italian original, later chapters and endnotes unread. Read selected passages of Cándida Smith’s review and Thompson’s interview; Scott’s foreword only through the publisher’s displayed excerpt. Gender and Memory reading covers original Introduction pp. 1–3 and selected edition preliminaries; its later chapters are unread. Bewes’s review and Passerini’s reply were read as displayed publisher excerpts, not complete articles. The women’s-history essay was read only in its opening extract and A Passion for Memory only in abstract. Selected other books were identified bibliographically and not read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987; Italian original 1984), Passerini retains Durkheim’s collective representations but criticizes their reification and insufficient attention to individual activity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 1–2: “collective representations”; p. 2 distinguishes an entity from a process. Publisher excerpt read; Durkheim’s cited text and book endnotes unread. Qualified criticism, not wholesale rejection.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987; Italian original 1984), Passerini sets her study against Febvre's call for a history of sensibilities and collective psychology, describing it as only a preliminary outline by that standard.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 3, paragraphs beginning A notable example and It is not difficult: “following Febvre’s directions”. Primary publisher excerpt read; exact Febvre edition not established from the unread notes.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini invokes Raymond Williams’s call for a critical study of past and present culture in defining her historical approach.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 3, paragraph beginning It is perhaps: “Raymond Williams noted”. Primary passage read; no particular Williams title supplied by the excerpt, and no claim of sole derivation.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini follows Gramsci’s treatment of folklore as a conception of the world to justify serious historical study of ordinary life stories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 4, opening paragraph: “Following what Gramsci wrote about folklore”. Primary publisher excerpt read; particular Gramsci edition and endnote unread. This is a stated methodological debt.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Fascism in Popular Memory (1987), Passerini questions the correspondence between individual interviewee and social stratum assumed in Thompson’s The Edwardians (1975), while recognizing their different research aims.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 10, section 3 The interviewees, paragraphs naming Essex and Thompson: “only partially compensated”. Page visually checked as well as OCR-read. Final paragraph distinguishes documenting social change from studying narrative forms; no total rejection of Thompson or general rejection of sampling claimed. The Edwardians itself unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In a retrospective interview (1996, 2002), Thompson says that by the second edition of The Voice of the Past (1988) oral historians had been very strongly influenced by Passerini's ideas on subjectivity, silence and memory, and he connects this to that edition's new chapter, "Memory and the Self".
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Karen Worcman interview (1996, 2002), UK Data Archive thematic highlights (June 2017), section 15, printed p. 13/PDF p. 16: “very strongly influenced both by Luisa Passerini”. Section 14, p. 12, contrasts the first edition. The same paragraph credits Portelli even more strongly; this new individual route preserves that mixed attribution. Existing edge_2974 is Portelli→Thompson, not Passerini→Thompson. The 1988 chapter is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott wrote the foreword to the English Autobiography of a Generation (1996; Italian original 1988), commending its way of approaching lived history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wesleyan publisher contents, Foreword by Joan Wallach Scott, and displayed foreword quotation: “closer to lived history”. This verifies an introduction and a bounded published appraisal; whole foreword unread. Scott is not asserted to have supervised Passerini.
proposed_edges.map_label: Scott’s foreword to the English memoir

proposed_edges.relationship: In "Discontinuity of History and Diaspora of Languages" (2000), Passerini names Hobsbawm as an inspiration and says his work was very important in her formation, while granting the gulf Bewes saw between her fragmentary exposition and his continuous narrative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, final displayed paragraph beginning As it happens: “one historian I have taken as an inspiration is Eric Hobsbawm”. No particular Hobsbawm work is identified in the read passage; no claim about agreement on every question or a supervisory relationship.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fascism in Popular Memory (1987) develops an oral-history method that interprets narrative form and the interview encounter alongside other historical sources.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 8–9: “pre-existing story-lines”. Read publisher excerpt distinguishes inherited narrative forms from interview effects, then discusses checking testimony against other sources. Whole book unread. Existing oral→memory and oral→political group edges are not direct person→oral edges.
proposed_edges.map_label: Narrative form and the interview encounter

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Passion for Memory” (2011), Passerini argues that a memory of Europe includes how Europe is remembered by others as well as what Europeans remember.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final two paragraphs: “Europe is the object”. Abstract only; full article unread. Claim is this stated extension of memory’s subject/object, not proof of reception or a founding role in memory studies.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Selma Leydesdorff and Paul Thompson, Passerini’s introduction to Gender and Memory (1996) asks how memory is gendered while warning against treating cultural distinctions as universal gender differences.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint Introduction, pp. 1–3 (licensed preview PDF pp. 20–22), especially p. 1: “transcultural essential gender differences”. Joint authorship explicit. Preview ends mid-sentence on p. 3; remainder unread. The separately authored new introduction in the 2005 edition belongs to Leydesdorff.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fascism in Popular Memory (1987) challenges labour histories that identify working-class subjectivity either with its organizations or with an inherently oppositional class.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, pp. 4–7, especially p. 6: “traditional Marxists”. Read primary excerpt addresses an explicit historiographical problem, not just workers as a shared topic. Claim concerns the Italian historiography described there, not all Marxist or labour history.

proposed_edges.relationship: “A Memory for Women’s History” (1992) describes an oral-history project accompanying the creation of an archive of recent feminism in Emilia-Romagna.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher extract, p. 669, opening two paragraphs: “an oral history project”. Supports the concrete contribution to documenting women’s movements; later argument and full article unread. Does not claim Passerini founded or solely created the independent Bologna archive.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Oral History Theory (first published 2010; second edition, 2016), Lynn Abrams uses Passerini’s Work Ideology and Consensus under Italian Fascism (1979) to explain why oral historians must investigate the production and cultural settings of remembered narratives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed second-edition preview. Abrams reconstructs Passerini’s interpretation of workers’ silences and discrepant recollections, then derives an interpretive obligation from it. The claim concerns this substantive methodological use; the 2010 edition was not separately read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Interpreting how memory narratives are produced

proposed_edges.relationship: In their introduction to Beyond Women’s Words (2018), Franca Iacovetta, Katrina Srigley and Stacey Zembrzycki draw on Passerini’s understanding of the interview as a social relationship and credit her argument that present circumstances help shape memories of the past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed preview’s introduction through its available p. 11. At p. 1 the authors invoke Passerini’s ‘social relationship that is the interview’; at p. 8 they explicitly credit her account of memory’s dependence on the present. This is a jointly authored conceptual uptake, not an inference from editorial co-credits. The endnotes are outside the preview, so no particular earlier Passerini publication is assigned to these statements.
proposed_edges.map_label: Interview relationships and memory in the present

proposed_edges.relationship: In Love and the Idea of Europe (2009; revised as Women and Men in Love, 2012), Passerini connected European political identity with the history of courtly and romantic love while questioning claims that this form of love belonged exclusively to European civilization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction, especially pp. 1–6. The opening explains her historical inquiry into political belonging and emotions and its critique of European exclusivity. This supports a specific contribution to the history of emotions. Edition years follow her institutional publication list, p. 2: 2009 for the earlier English title and 2012 for the revision. The publisher also lists a December 2008 hardback release. The rest of the book was not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Love, political identity and European exclusivity
